nodes.label: Scope: no identifying mark
nodes.text: The dispute concerns ordinary lost objects without an identifying mark.
nodes.hebrew: כי פליגי בדבר שאין בו סימן

nodes.label: Marked objects: agreement
nodes.text: Both reject unconscious yeush here; later despair does not repair an already prohibited pickup.

nodes.label: Sea / river exception
nodes.text: The Torah permits the exceptional sea or river loss, even with a mark.

nodes.label: Abaye: no awareness
nodes.text: The owner has not yet learned of the loss.

nodes.label: Abaye: ineffective
nodes.text: Unconscious yeush is not effective in the disputed case.

nodes.label: Rava: future despair
nodes.text: Once aware, the owner will despair because there is no identifying mark.

nodes.label: Rava: effective now
nodes.text: In the disputed case, that anticipated despair counts now.

nodes.label: Scattered coins: permitted
nodes.text: The cited Mishnah lets the finder keep scattered coins.

nodes.label: Objection: owner unaware
nodes.text: The objection assumes that the owner has not learned of this loss.

nodes.label: Bridge: test Abaye
nodes.text: If permission holds while awareness is absent, this case conflicts with Abaye.

nodes.label: Coins challenge
nodes.text: Permission plus assumed unawareness challenges Abaye, using the stated bridge.

nodes.label: Reply: purse checking
nodes.text: People habitually check their purses, says Rabbi Yitzhak.

nodes.label: Owner already knew
nodes.text: The reply treats the owner as aware and despairing before the finder picked up the coins.

nodes.label: Coins do not decide
nodes.text: With unawareness denied, the coins case does not establish Rava over Abaye.

nodes.label: Verse: loss from you
nodes.text: Deuteronomy 22:3 is read as addressing loss from the owner that remains accessible to others.

nodes.label: Inaccessible loss: permitted
nodes.text: A river loss inaccessible to everyone is excluded from that obligation.
nodes.hebrew: שאבודה ממנו ואינה מצויה אצל כל אדם

nodes.label: Compare both categories
nodes.text: The Gemara compares prohibition and permission: each covers items with or without a mark.

nodes.label: Clarify: before awareness
nodes.text: For the ordinary-loss prohibition, the owner has not learned of the loss before pickup.

nodes.label: River comparison
nodes.text: Apply the comparison to ordinary unmarked loss before awareness: anticipated despair does not permit it.

nodes.label: Ordinary loss: still prohibited
nodes.text: In that unaware-before-pickup case, ordinary recoverable loss is prohibited even without a mark.

nodes.label: Rava: explicitly refuted
nodes.text: The Gemara declares the refutation of Rava decisive.

nodes.label: Ruling: follows Abaye
nodes.text: The text rules for Abaye here, within the mnemonic YAAL KAGAM.
